vignette: The phone call still arrives in her dreams before it ever reaches her bedside. Three years ago, the dispatcher describes the crumpled sedan, the shattered glass, and the quiet certainty that her daughter, Mai, will not wake up. Hine remembers the weight of her service radio against her hip as she navigates the precinct parking lot in her unmarked car, the wipers fighting a Pacific downpour that no longer seems to stop. She drives past the same curve twice before the navigation speaks the street name. At the hospital, the fluorescent lights hum like trapped wasps. Mai survives, but the long road to recovery begins with nights spent in plastic chairs, watching the rhythmic blink of monitors, listening to the sterile cadence of nurses' boots. Hine's hands, once steady enough to clear a chaotic scene, now tremble when she signs her name. Time does not smooth the edges of that evening. Now seventy-one, Hine still wears the weight of those months in the tightness across her shoulders and the way she scans every room before she sits. She counts the exits on instinct, her eyes tracking the clock, the doors, the faces of strangers. When Mai's recovery stalls, when a familiar scent of antiseptic drifts from a neighbor's medicine cabinet, Hine's breath catches. She stops at crosswalks longer than necessary, gripping the steering wheel until her knuckles bleach. Sleep fractures into the sound of grinding metal, and she wakes with her heart hammering against her ribs, certain she is still rushing toward an address that exists only in memory. Her husband, Kiri, leaves a hand on her back sometimes, but she flinches before she can remember to lean into the touch. At seventy-one, Hine remains on the force, assigned to community liaison duties that still require her to sit in the back of her patrol car and respond to calls in her district. Colleagues know not to ask about the overtime, the extra checks, the way she memorizes every resident's license plate on her route. She listens to the radio static with a quiet intensity, her voice level when she speaks, her movements precise. But the work pulls at something raw. When a siren wails down the street, her stomach drops. She finds herself replaying Mai's hospital room while processing a minor traffic stop, the boundary between then and now thinning until her pulse matches the radio's crackle. She drinks her tea black, watches the garden gate every time it clicks, and keeps the living room quiet, fearing that loud voices might shatter the fragile peace she has spent years rebuilding. The grief does not announce itself; it settles. It lives in the way she pauses before Mai's voicemail, in the careful way she folds laundry to avoid creasing anything that reminds her of hospital blankets, in the quiet exhaustion that follows a full day of pretending she is not constantly waiting for the other shoe to fall. She loves her husband, her work, her neighborhood, but the trauma has carved a parallel track through her days, one where the past never truly passes, only waits. She breathes, she walks, she signs her name, and she continues to show up, carrying the weight without asking anyone to notice how heavy it has become.
